<reason>Both sides opened well and stayed disciplined with evidence. A built a morally compelling case (consent fiction, structural invisible harm, presumption analogies) and landed excellent turns — the Apple prompt as opt-in-working, the loyalty programs as the industry's "confession." But B did more decisive rebuttal work: the coercion dilemma (if services are essential, an opt-in "yes" is coerced by the same logic), the job-acceptance reductio of A's costless-refusal consent test, the ATT consolidation counter, and "decoupling is a hope, not a mechanism" — none of which A ever squarely absorbed. B also answered both pressure questions concretely (loyalty programs and free-tier choices as affirmative consent; regulator-initiated audits analogous to food and financial inspection), while A's answers leaned on asserted decoupling and a hand-wavy "shared consent infrastructure" that B convincingly rebranded as Google/Apple login buttons. A's closing was rhetorically superb but crystallized the moral frame while leaving B's mechanistic hits standing. B made the debate easier to decide: A's rule promises a costless "no" it cannot deliver, at regressive cost, where targeted enforcement reaches the actual harms.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1/2 sequence culminating in the coercion trilemma: the job-acceptance reductio ("consent given against a background cost is still consent — that is what trade is") plus "nothing in the motion guarantees you keep the email, the maps, the search" exposed that A's promised costless refusal is asserted rather than delivered — pressure A never directly answered in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
